title: Coherent Control of Domain-Wall Transport in an Ultracold Bose Gas
authors: O. Farion, M. Pourzand, J. M. McGuirk
abstract: Domain walls are carriers of spin transport whose controlled manipulation underlies a wide range of spintronic and information-processing technologies. Here we demonstrate tunable domain-wall transport in a weakly interacting nondegenerate ultracold Bose gas. We initialize a three-domain pseudo-spin-1/2 texture and observe spontaneous propagation of long-lived domain walls driven by exchange-mediated spin currents. By varying the orientation of the spin domains, we control the balance of spin currents across the walls and thereby tune their trajectories, including reversals of the initial direction of motion. Measurements reveal a crossover from an exchange-stabilized regime, in which coherent spin-exchange collisions suppress wall motion, to a diffusion-dominated regime characterized by rapid transport at thermal velocities. Numerical solutions of a quantum Boltzmann equation reproduce the observed dynamics and identify transverse phase gradients as an important control parameter governing domain-wall propagation. These results establish coherence and phase engineering as tools for programming spin transport in ultracold gases and provide a route toward controllable domain-wall dynamics in atomtronic systems.
summary: The authors demonstrate precise, tunable control over the movement of magnetic domain walls within a Bose gas by engineering the system's spin coherence and phase structure. They show that manipulating initial polarization can reverse or accelerate wall motion, confirming that coherence acts as a powerful tool for programming spin transport in atomtronic devices.
main_problem: The central challenge is demonstrating and controlling domain-wall transport, which act as carriers of spin information, using coherence and phase engineering in an ultracold gas.
main_result: Tunable control over domain-wall motion—including reversal and acceleration—is achieved by manipulating the spin current imbalance through polarization rotation. The dynamics exhibit a crossover between exchange-stabilized and diffusion-dominated regimes.
method: The study combines experimental measurements (absorption imaging, Ramsey spectroscopy) to track magnetization profiles with numerical solutions of a quantum Boltzmann equation to model the underlying physics.
model_or_system: The system is a weakly interacting nondegenerate ultracold Bose gas ($	ext{}^{87}	ext{Rb}$) trapped in 1D, forming a pseudo-spin-1/2 texture between two hyperfine ground states. The dynamics are modeled using a quantum Boltzmann equation for the magnetization density.
key_observables: Domain wall trajectories, longitudinal magnetization ($M_{\parallel}$), transverse spin magnitude and phase ($\phi$), and domain wall velocity ($v_{dw}$).
important_parameters: Polarization rotation ($P$), transverse phase gradients ($\partial z\phi$), and the balance between exchange-stabilized and diffusion-dominated regimes.
main_assumptions: The analysis initially focused on domains with negative initial positions, and extremely small domain wall widths were avoided due to the Castaing instability.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the spatiotemporal evolution of magnetization profiles, showing how polarization rotation controls trajectories (including reversals), and map out the crossover in domain-wall velocity between slow/exchange-stabilized and fast/diffusive regimes.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical platform and problem, details measurement techniques for spin textures, presents results demonstrating control via coherence and phase engineering, models the dynamics using a quantum Boltzmann equation, and concludes by establishing the utility of this method for atomtronic systems.
why_interesting: This work directly applies concepts from non-equilibrium many-body physics (like domain wall dynamics) to an ultracold atomic platform, providing concrete experimental evidence for programming spin transport using coherence—a key area in AMO and quantum simulation.
